chapters.title: Modeling
chapters.tagline: The falling penny myth, and the loop every model goes through
goals: Describe the modeling loop: abstraction, analysis or simulation, validation
Compute the fall of a penny from the Empire State Building, and say why the answer is wrong
Write small Python functions with parameters and return values

blocks.html:
You may have heard that a penny dropped from the top of the Empire State Building would hit the sidewalk hard enough to kill someone. Is it true? We answer in stages, and the stages are the lesson.

Modeling means choosing which details of the real world to keep and which to leave out (abstraction), working out what the model predicts (by analysis with math, or by simulation with a computer), and then checking the prediction against reality (validation). When the model fails, you go around again with a better one.

blocks.q: Which step of the modeling loop checks whether a model's predictions agree with the real world?
blocks.why: Validation compares results to measurements. Abstraction decides what to include; analysis and simulation produce the predictions.

sections.title: A first model: ignore the air

blocks.html:
The simplest model: the penny falls with constant acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² and nothing slows it. The building is about h = 381 m tall. Kinematics gives

  • time to fall: t = √(2h / g)
  • speed at the bottom: v = √(2 g h)

blocks.code:
g = 9.8      # m/s**2
h = 381      # m
t = sqrt(2 * h / g)
v = sqrt(2 * g * h)
print(f"fall time: {t:.1f} s")
print(f"impact speed: {v:.1f} m/s  ({v * 3.6:.0f} km/h)")
blocks.title: How fast, how long?

blocks.code:
g = 9.8
h = 0.5 * g * 2**2
print(h)
print(sqrt(2 * g * h))

blocks.title: Fall from any height
blocks.prompt: Write fall(h, g=9.8) returning a tuple (t, v): the time to fall height h and the speed at the bottom, ignoring air resistance. sqrt is available from the prelude.
blocks.tests:
t, v = fall(381)
assert abs(t - 8.82) < 0.01 and abs(v - 86.4) < 0.1, f"Empire State Building: about 8.8 s and 86 m/s, got {t:.2f}, {v:.2f}"
t2, v2 = fall(4.9)
assert abs(t2 - 1.0) < 1e-9, "4.9 m takes exactly 1 s"
assert abs(fall(10, g=1.6)[0] - sqrt(12.5)) < 1e-9, "Use the g you are given (the Moon: 1.6)"
hints: Return both values separated by a comma: return t, v.
blocks.starter:
def fall(h, g=9.8):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def fall(h, g=9.8):
    t = sqrt(2 * h / g)
    v = sqrt(2 * g * h)
    return t, v

blocks.title: Time and distance to reach a speed
blocks.tests:
t, h = time_to_speed(9.8)
assert abs(t - 1) < 1e-9 and abs(h - 4.9) < 1e-9, "Reaching 9.8 m/s takes 1 s and 4.9 m"
assert abs(time_to_speed(18)[1] - 18**2 / (2 * 9.8)) < 1e-9, "A penny reaches 18 m/s after falling v²/2g, about 16.5 m"

blocks.html: 86 m/s is about 300 km/h, so a penny would be dangerous. But the real answer, from experiments, is that a falling penny reaches only about 18 m/s and stings rather than kills. The model left out air resistance: once the penny is fast enough, drag balances gravity and it stops speeding up (its terminal velocity). You'll build that better model in chapter 21.

blocks.name: ms-penny
blocks.title: Drop the penny
blocks.goal: From the 381 m tower, drop the penny with no air, then with air, and compare both with the measured speed.
blocks.intro: Two models of the same fall. The plot keeps every drop so you can compare them.

blocks.q: The no-air model predicts 86 m/s; measurements say about 18 m/s. What's the right response?

opts.t: Trust the math; the experiments must be wrong
Go back to abstraction and add the missing physics (drag), then check again

blocks.why: A failed validation tells you which simplification mattered. Here, ignoring air resistance was fine for a short drop but not for 381 m. Iterate: add drag, predict, validate again.

blocks.title: Time to terminal speed
blocks.prompt: A rough second model: the penny falls freely until it reaches its terminal speed of 18 m/s, then keeps that speed. Fill in the blanks to compute the total time to fall h metres.
blocks.tests:
t = fall_with_terminal(381)
assert abs(t - 22.1) < 0.1, f"About 22 s for the Empire State Building, got {t:.2f}"
assert abs(fall_with_terminal(100, v_term=10, g=10) - 10.5) < 1e-9, "1 s to reach 10 m/s covering 5 m, then 95 m at 10 m/s"
hints: Free fall from rest: distance = ½·g·t².
blocks.starter:
def fall_with_terminal(h, v_term=18, g=9.8):
    t1 = v_term / g              # time to reach terminal speed
    h1 = ____                    # distance fallen in that time
    t2 = ____                    # time for the rest at constant speed
    return t1 + t2
blocks.solution:
def fall_with_terminal(h, v_term=18, g=9.8):
    t1 = v_term / g
    h1 = 0.5 * g * t1**2
    t2 = (h - h1) / v_term
    return t1 + t2

blocks.q: Describe the modeling loop this course uses, with the penny as the example.
blocks.a:
• Abstraction: decide what to include (gravity) and what to leave out (air).
  • Analysis/simulation: compute the prediction (86 m/s, 8.8 s).
  • Validation: compare with measurements (about 18 m/s), find the model is wrong.
  • Iterate: add the missing piece (drag), predict and validate again.

sections.title: Real-world project: a drop-zone safety check

blocks.html: The modeling loop isn't only for pennies. Building sites have to decide where people may walk below workers on scaffolding, and the question is the same one you just answered: how fast does a dropped object hit the ground? Your two models give two answers. The no-air model is the cautious one (it never underestimates), and the terminal-speed model is the realistic one, if you know the object's terminal speed.

blocks.title: Drop-zone safety check for a building site
blocks.client: A construction company putting up a 12-storey block
blocks.brief: The site manager has a list of work platforms (heights in metres) and a list of tools that could fall, each with a measured terminal speed. Anything that hits the ground faster than 15 m/s needs safety netting under that platform. Write the code that says, for every platform, how fast the worst tool lands and whether netting is required.
blocks.why: Engineers do exactly this when they write safety rules: start with a simple model, check it against measurements, and choose the model that is safe enough for the decision. The same "simple bound first, better model later" habit shows up in capacity planning, timeouts in web servers ("assume the slowest case"), and any code that has to be safe before it is precise.
milestones: Write impact_speed(h, v_term): free-fall speed, but never more than the terminal speed
Check it: a low platform gives the free-fall answer, a high one gives the terminal speed
Write netting_plan(heights, terminal_speeds, limit) that marks each platform as needing netting or not
Print the plan as a table the site manager can read
Compare: how many platforms would the no-air model have flagged?
stretch: Add the fall time to the table, so workers know how long a warning shout has
Let each platform have its own list of tools instead of one shared list
Plot impact speed against height for both models on one chart

blocks.title: impact_speed with a terminal cap
blocks.prompt: Write impact_speed(h, v_term, g=9.8): the speed at the bottom of a fall of h metres. Use the free-fall formula √(2·g·h), but an object can never go faster than its terminal speed v_term, so return whichever is smaller.
blocks.tests:
assert impact_speed(5, 40) is not None, "Return the speed, don't print it"
assert abs(impact_speed(5, 40) - sqrt(98)) < 1e-9, f"5 m: free fall gives about 9.9 m/s, below the cap of 40. Got {impact_speed(5, 40)}"
assert impact_speed(381, 18) == 18, "The penny from the Empire State Building: capped at 18 m/s"
assert abs(impact_speed(10, 30, g=1.6) - sqrt(32)) < 1e-9, "Use the g you are given"
hints: min(a, b) returns the smaller of two numbers.
blocks.starter:
def impact_speed(h, v_term, g=9.8):
    pass

blocks.title: netting_plan
blocks.prompt: Write netting_plan(heights, terminal_speeds, limit=15). For each platform height, find the fastest impact among all the tools (use impact_speed, which is provided). Return a list of (height, speed, needs_net) tuples, where needs_net is True when the speed is above limit.
blocks.setup:
def impact_speed(h, v_term, g=9.8):
    return min(sqrt(2 * g * h), v_term)
blocks.tests:
plan = netting_plan([2, 20], [9, 25])
assert len(plan) == 2, f"One row per platform, got {len(plan)}"
h, v, net = plan[0]
assert h == 2 and abs(v - sqrt(39.2)) < 1e-9 and not net, f"2 m: the worst tool lands at about 6.3 m/s, no net needed. Got {plan[0]}"
h, v, net = plan[1]
assert abs(v - sqrt(392)) < 1e-9 and net, f"20 m: the hammer (terminal 25) lands at about 19.8 m/s, net needed. Got {plan[1]}"
assert not netting_plan([50], [9, 12])[0][2], "Light tools capped below 15 m/s never need a net, even from high up"
hints: For one height, max(impact_speed(h, v) for v in terminal_speeds) is the worst case.

blocks.title: The cap that never caps
blocks.prompt: This version says a tool dropped from 1 m hits the floor at 40 m/s. Find the bug.
blocks.tests:
assert abs(impact_speed(5, 40) - sqrt(98)) < 1e-9, f"5 m of free fall gives about 9.9 m/s, below the cap of 40. Got {impact_speed(5, 40)}"
assert impact_speed(381, 18) == 18, "From 381 m the penny is capped at 18 m/s"
hints: Terminal speed is a ceiling. The object goes as fast as free fall allows, but never faster than the cap: take the smaller of the two.

chapters.title: Bike share
chapters.tagline: State objects, functions, if statements and for loops, all around two bike stations
goals: Represent a system's state with a State object and change it
Write functions with parameters, and use flip to model random arrivals
Run a simulation in a for loop and record results in a TimeSeries
Plot the results

blocks.html:
Olin College and Wellesley College share a small bike system. People ride bikes between the two campuses. The question that drives the next three chapters: how many bikes should be at each station so riders rarely find one empty?

The model's state is the number of bikes at each station. ModSim's State object holds named state variables you can read and change as attributes.

blocks.code:
bikeshare = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
print(bikeshare)
print("bikes at Olin:", bikeshare.olin)
bikeshare.olin -= 1
bikeshare.wellesley += 1
print("after one ride:", bikeshare.olin, bikeshare.wellesley)
blocks.title: A State object

blocks.code:
bikeshare = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
bikeshare.olin -= 3
bikeshare.wellesley = bikeshare.wellesley + 3
print(bikeshare.olin, bikeshare.wellesley)
print(bikeshare.olin + bikeshare.wellesley)

blocks.title: bike_to_wellesley and bike_to_olin
blocks.prompt: Write the two functions. Each takes the state, moves one bike, and returns nothing (it changes the state in place).
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
bike_to_wellesley(s)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (9, 3), f"After one ride to Wellesley: (9, 3), got {(s.olin, s.wellesley)}"
bike_to_olin(s); bike_to_olin(s)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (11, 1), "Two rides back to Olin: (11, 1)"

blocks.html: We don't know when people will want a bike, so the model uses probabilities. Each minute, a customer arrives at Olin with probability p1 and at Wellesley with probability p2. ModSim's flip(p) returns True with probability p.

blocks.code:
results = [flip(0.7) for i in range(20)]
print(results)
print("fraction True:", sum(results) / len(results))
blocks.title: flip
step
blocks.prompt: Fill in the if statements so step simulates one minute: with probability p1 a bike goes to Wellesley, and with probability p2 a bike goes to Olin. The two ride functions are defined.
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
step(s, 1, 0)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (9, 3), "p1 = 1, p2 = 0: one bike must go to Wellesley"
step(s, 0, 1)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (10, 2), "p1 = 0, p2 = 1: one bike back to Olin"
step(s, 0, 0)

bikeshare = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
olin, wellesley = TimeSeries(), TimeSeries()
for i in range(60):
    step(bikeshare, 0.4, 0.2)
    olin[i], wellesley[i] = bikeshare.olin, bikeshare.wellesley
plot(olin, label="Olin"); plot(wellesley, label="Wellesley")
decorate(title="An hour of rides, driven by your step()", xlabel="Time step (min)", ylabel="Number of bikes")

blocks.title: The bikes that vanish
blocks.prompt: After a few rides back to Olin, the total number of bikes keeps dropping. Find the bug.
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
bike_to_olin(s)
assert s.olin + s.wellesley == 12, f"A ride moves a bike, so the total stays 12. Got {s.olin + s.wellesley}"

sections.title: Run it and record the results

blocks.html: A for loop runs step once per minute. To plot what happened, store the state after each minute in a TimeSeries, which maps a time to a value.

blocks.name: ms-bike
blocks.title: Run the bike stations
blocks.goal: Run an hour a few times, then raise p1 until a station goes below zero.
blocks.intro: Riders arrive at random each minute. Faint lines keep earlier runs.

blocks.title: Run for an hour and record Olin's bikes
blocks.tests: assert len(results) == 61 and results[0] == 10

blocks.code:
def step(state, p1, p2):
    if flip(p1):
        state.olin -= 1; state.wellesley += 1
    if flip(p2):
        state.wellesley -= 1; state.olin += 1

bikeshare = State(olin=10, wellesley=2)
results = TimeSeries()
results[0] = bikeshare.olin
for i in range(60):
    step(bikeshare, 0.4, 0.2)
    results[i + 1] = bikeshare.olin

plot(results, label="Olin")
decorate(title="Olin-Wellesley bikeshare", xlabel="Time step (min)", ylabel="Number of bikes")
print("bikes at Olin after an hour:", results[60])
blocks.title: Plot the hour

blocks.html: Run it a few times: each run is different. Then set p1 = 0.6. What goes wrong?

blocks.q: With p1 = 0.6 and p2 = 0.2, the plot can dip below zero. What does that tell you?

opts.t: The model allows impossible states: it lets people take bikes from an empty station

blocks.why: Real stations can't have −2 bikes. The model needs a rule: if a station is empty, the customer leaves without a bike. Chapter 3 adds that check and counts the unhappy customers.

blocks.q: What are the state, the parameters, and the randomness in the bike share model?
blocks.a:
• State: the number of bikes at Olin and at Wellesley (a State object).
  • Parameters: p1 and p2, the per-minute probabilities of a customer at each station.
  • Randomness: flip(p) decides each minute whether a customer arrives, so every run differs.

sections.title: Real-world project: a scooter rebalancing schedule

blocks.html: Bike and scooter companies really do run this model. Every morning commuters ride from the suburbs into downtown, and every evening they ride back, so scooters pile up in one place and run out in the other. A van drives around at night moving them back. The company's question is our question: how many should be in each zone at the start of the day?

blocks.title: Overnight rebalancing plan for an e-scooter fleet
blocks.client: A scooter-sharing startup with two zones, Downtown and Riverside
blocks.brief: The company has hourly ride counts for a typical weekday: how many scooters leave Downtown for Riverside and how many come back, hour by hour. Use them to simulate a day, record Downtown's stock in a TimeSeries, and work out the smallest number of scooters the van must leave Downtown overnight so neither zone ever runs out.
blocks.why: This is real fleet-operations software: bike share (Citi Bike, Santander Cycles), scooter companies and car-sharing all run nightly rebalancing jobs. The same pattern, "replay the demand and find the lowest starting stock that never hits zero", is how shops set reorder levels and how cloud teams size a pool of servers before a busy period.
milestones: Write run_day(state, moves) that applies each hour's rides and records Downtown's stock
Plot one day and spot the hour Downtown is emptiest
Write min_start(moves, total): the smallest overnight stock at Downtown that keeps both zones at 0 or above
Turn it into a plan: "move N scooters to Downtown tonight"
Re-run with a rainy-day demand list and compare the plans
stretch: Add a third zone and a van that can carry only 20 scooters per trip
Use flip to make the demand random and find a start that works on 95% of simulated days
Count how many rides you'd lose if the van skipped a night

blocks.title: run_day for two zones
blocks.prompt: Write run_day(state, moves). state is a State(downtown=..., riverside=...). moves is a list of (out, back) pairs, one per hour: out scooters ride Downtown → Riverside, then back ride Riverside → Downtown. Change the state in place, and return a TimeSeries of Downtown's stock: index 0 holds the starting stock and index h + 1 holds the stock after hour h.
blocks.tests:
s = State(downtown=10, riverside=5)
r = run_day(s, [(3, 1), (0, 4)])
assert len(r) == 3, f"Start plus one value per hour: 3 values, got {len(r)}"
assert r.tolist() == [10, 8, 12], f"Downtown: 10, then 10-3+1 = 8, then 8+4 = 12. Got {r.tolist()}"
assert (s.downtown, s.riverside) == (12, 3), "The state itself should end at 12 and 3"
assert s.downtown + s.riverside == 15, "Scooters are moved, never created or lost"
hints: for h, (out, back) in enumerate(moves): gives you the hour number and the two counts at once.
blocks.solution:
def run_day(state, moves):
    results = TimeSeries()
    results[0] = state.downtown
    for h, (out, back) in enumerate(moves):
        state.downtown -= out
        state.riverside += out
        state.riverside -= back
        state.downtown += back
        results[h + 1] = state.downtown
    return results

blocks.title: min_start for the van
blocks.prompt: Write min_start(moves, total): the smallest number of scooters to leave at Downtown overnight (the other total - start go to Riverside) so that after every hour both zones have 0 or more. Try start = 0, 1, 2, …, total in order and return the first that works, or None if none does. run_day is provided.
blocks.setup:
def run_day(state, moves):
    results = TimeSeries()
    results[0] = state.downtown
    for h, (out, back) in enumerate(moves):
        state.downtown += back - out
        state.riverside += out - back
        results[h + 1] = state.downtown
    return results
blocks.tests:
morning = [(6, 1), (5, 0), (2, 3)]
assert min_start(morning, 20) == 10, f"Downtown drops by 5 then 5 more, so it needs at least 10. Got {min_start(morning, 20)}"
evening = [(0, 4), (1, 6)]
assert min_start(evening, 12) == 0, "When riders come back to Downtown, it can start empty"
assert min_start(evening, 8) is None, "Riverside needs 9 for the evening rush; with only 8 scooters no start works"
hints: Riverside's stock at every hour is total - downtown, so (total - r).min() is its lowest point.

chapters.title: Iterative modeling
chapters.tagline: Fix the negative bikes, count unhappy customers, and document what you write
goals: Improve a model one small change at a time and re-check it
Use comparison operators and early return to guard against impossible states
Add metrics (counters in the state) that measure how well the system works

sections.title: Iterate: one small improvement at a time

blocks.html: Chapter 2's model let stations go negative. The approach: don't redesign everything; make the smallest change that fixes the problem, run it, check it. That's iterative modeling.

blocks.q: Why do we build the bike model in many small steps instead of writing the whole thing at once?

opts.t: Each small change can be tested immediately, so when something breaks you know which change caused it
Big programs can't use random numbers

blocks.why: Small steps keep the program working at every stage. When a test fails, the bug is in the few lines you just changed.

blocks.html: The fix needs a test: "is the station empty?" Python's comparison operators return True or False: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Careful: = assigns, == compares.

blocks.code:
olin = 0
print(olin == 0, olin != 0, olin > 0)
olin = 3
print(olin >= 3 and olin < 10)

blocks.title: Guard the empty station
blocks.prompt: Fill the blanks so bike_to_wellesley does nothing when Olin has no bikes. An early return leaves the function immediately.
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=0, wellesley=12)
bike_to_wellesley(s)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (0, 12), "An empty station can't lend a bike"
s = State(olin=1, wellesley=0)
bike_to_wellesley(s)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (0, 1), "With one bike, the ride happens"

blocks.html: To compare designs we need a number that says how well the system works: a metric. We add two counters to the state: olin_empty and wellesley_empty, the number of customers who found an empty station.

blocks.title: Count the disappointed
blocks.prompt: Write both ride functions with guards and metrics: when a customer finds an empty station, add 1 to that station's _empty counter and return without moving a bike. Include a one-line docstring in each function.
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=1, wellesley=0, olin_empty=0, wellesley_empty=0)
bike_to_olin(s)
assert s.wellesley_empty == 1 and (s.olin, s.wellesley) == (1, 0), "Empty Wellesley: count it, move nothing"
bike_to_wellesley(s); bike_to_wellesley(s)
assert (s.olin, s.wellesley, s.olin_empty) == (0, 1, 1), "One ride, then one unhappy customer at Olin"
assert bike_to_olin.__doc__ and bike_to_wellesley.__doc__, "Add a docstring to each function"
hints: A docstring is a string literal on the first line of the function body: """What it does.""".
blocks.solution:
def bike_to_wellesley(state):
    """Move one bike from Olin to Wellesley, or count an unhappy customer."""
    if state.olin == 0:
        state.olin_empty += 1
        return
    state.olin -= 1
    state.wellesley += 1

def bike_to_olin(state):
    """Move one bike from Wellesley to Olin, or count an unhappy customer."""
    if state.wellesley == 0:
        state.wellesley_empty += 1
        return
    state.wellesley -= 1
    state.olin += 1

blocks.title: Run an afternoon and count the unhappy
blocks.tests:
assert state.olin + state.wellesley == 12, "Bikes are moved, never lost"
assert state.olin >= 0 and state.wellesley >= 0, "The guards keep both stations at 0 or above"
assert unhappy == state.olin_empty + state.wellesley_empty, "Add up both stations' unhappy customers"

blocks.title: The vanishing-bikes bug
blocks.prompt: After this change, the total number of bikes in the system slowly shrinks. Bikes shouldn't disappear. Find the bug.
blocks.tests:
s = State(olin=5, wellesley=0, olin_empty=0, wellesley_empty=0)
bike_to_olin(s)
assert s.olin + s.wellesley == 5, f"Total bikes must stay 5, got {s.olin + s.wellesley}"
assert s.wellesley_empty == 1, "The customer is still counted"
hints: Without a return, the function keeps going after it counts the unhappy customer, and the "fix" afterwards hides the evidence while an extra bike appears at Olin.
blocks.solution:
def bike_to_olin(state):
    """Move one bike from Wellesley to Olin."""
    if state.wellesley == 0:
        state.wellesley_empty += 1
        return
    state.wellesley -= 1
    state.olin += 1

blocks.name: ms-bike-guard
blocks.title: Fix the negative bikes
blocks.goal: With the empty check on, run an hour that turns riders away, and see the stations stay at 0 or above.
blocks.intro: The same riders run through two rules: chapter 2's, and the fix.

blocks.title: Two hours, with metrics

blocks.q: What is a metric, and which metrics does the bike model use?
blocks.a:
• A metric is a number computed from a simulation that measures how well the system works, so you can compare designs or parameters.
  • The bike model counts olin_empty and wellesley_empty: customers who arrived at an empty station.

sections.title: Real-world project: drivers turned away at an EV charging hub

blocks.html: An empty bike station and a full car charger are the same problem in disguise: a customer shows up and the thing they want isn't there. The fix is the same too: guard against the impossible state (more cars charging than there are chargers) and count the people you had to turn away, because that count is the number the business decides with.

blocks.title: How many chargers does the motorway services need?
blocks.client: A motorway service station installing electric-car chargers
blocks.brief: The operator has a log from a busy Saturday: a string where A means a car arrived wanting to charge and L means a car finished and left. Build a model with a State holding free chargers and a turned_away counter, replay the log, and report how many drivers left without charging for 4, 6 and 8 chargers.
blocks.why: Counting failed requests is the core metric of real systems: "requests dropped" on a web server, "calls that got a busy signal" at a call centre, "orders we couldn't fill" in a warehouse. blocks.html: A function that prints its answer can't be used by other code. A function that returns its answer can be called in a loop, stored, plotted and tested. Every function from here on returns its results.

blocks.code:
def add_print(a, b):
    print(a + b)

def add_return(a, b):
    return a + b

x = add_print(2, 3)
y = add_return(2, 3)
print(x, y)

blocks.q: In the prediction above, why is x equal to None?

opts.t: add_print has no return statement, so calling it evaluates to None (it only displays the sum)

blocks.why: A function without return returns None. The 5 appeared on screen, but no value came back to store in x.

blocks.q: What does "sweeping a parameter" mean, and why is it useful?
blocks.a:
• Running the same model many times while varying one parameter over a range, and recording a metric for each value.
  • It shows how sensitive the results are to the parameter, finds ranges where the system works well or badly, and supports decisions (e.g. how many bikes to put at each station).

sections.title: Real-world project: how many meals should the food truck prep?

blocks.html: A sweep turns "it depends" into a chart you can decide from. Here the parameter isn't a probability but a choice the owner makes every morning: how many meals to cook. Too few and customers leave hungry; too many and food goes in the bin. Run the day once for each choice, measure the money, and the best choice is the top of the curve.

blocks.title: Daily prep quantity for a food truck
blocks.client: A taco truck that cooks everything before it opens
blocks.brief: Each taco plate sells for $9 and costs $3 to make. Unsold plates are thrown away. The owner has written down how many people wanted a plate on 10 recent days. Write day_profit for one day, then sweep the number of plates prepped from 40 to 120 and find the quantity with the best average profit over those days.
blocks.why: This is the classic "newsvendor" problem, and real software solves it every day: bakeries and supermarkets decide how much fresh food to order, airlines decide how many seats to overbook, cloud teams decide how many servers to keep warm. The tool is always the same: a function that scores one choice, swept over all the choices.

p_0 = get_first_value(census)

blocks.q: The constant-growth line matches both ends but runs above the data around 1950–1970 and below it around 1990. What does that suggest?

opts.t: Growth per year wasn't constant: it was smaller early on and larger later

blocks.why: Fitting the endpoints forces the line through them; the systematic misses in between tell you the real growth rate changed over time. Chapter 6 tries growth proportional to population.

blocks.title: The off-by-one bug
blocks.prompt: This loop is supposed to produce one value per year from t_0 to t_end inclusive, but the final year is missing and the plot stops short. Fix it.
blocks.tests:

assert get_last_label(r) == 2016, f"The last year should be 2016, got {get_last_label(r)}"
assert len(r) == 67, "1950 through 2016 is 67 values"
hints: linrange already excludes its stop value, and each pass computes t + 1.

blocks.q: Describe the constant-growth model: how its one parameter is chosen and how the simulation works.
blocks.a:
• Parameter: annual_growth = (p_end − p_0)/(t_end − t_0), chosen so the model matches the first and last data points.
  • Simulation: start with results[t_0] = p_0; for each year t, results[t+1] = results[t] + annual_growth.
  • It's a straight line; it misses the curvature in the data.

sections.title: Real-world project: will the town's school be full?

blocks.html: A constant-growth model is too simple for the whole world, but it is exactly what many small planning offices use for the next few years: take the trend from the records you have, carry it forward, and see when you hit a limit. The answer isn't certain, but it tells you when to start worrying, and that is often the decision.

blocks.title: School enrolment forecast for a growing town
blocks.client: The education office of a commuter town with one secondary school
blocks.brief: The school has 1,100 places. Enrolment was 812 in 2016 and has been rising as new houses are built. Using the records the office gives you, fit a constant-growth model, extend it ten years beyond the data, and report the first year the forecast goes over capacity, so the council knows when the new wing must open.
blocks.why: Trend projection like this is everywhere in planning software: school places, hospital beds, road traffic, warehouse space, even "when will this disk fill up?" alerts in server monitoring. The skill is the same: fit the simplest model to the data, project it, and find where it crosses a limit.
milestones: Load the enrolment records into a TimeSeries and plot them
Write forecast(series, end_year): carry the average annual growth forward from the last record
Write first_year_over(series, capacity): the first year a forecast exceeds capacity, or None
Plot records, forecast and a horizontal capacity line together
Re-fit using only the last 4 years: does the warning year move? Which would you trust?

blocks.title: forecast enrolment
blocks.prompt: Write forecast(series, end_year). Compute the average annual growth from the first and last points of series (as in this chapter). Then return a new TimeSeries that starts at the last data year with the last data value and adds that growth each year up to and including end_year.
blocks.tests:
records = TimeSeries({2012: 700.0, 2014: 760.0, 2016: 812.0})
f = forecast(records, 2026)
assert get_first_label(f) == 2016 and f[2016] == 812, "Start from the last record: 2016, 812 pupils"
assert get_last_label(f) == 2026, f"Go up to and including 2026, got {get_last_label(f)}"
assert abs(f[2017] - 840) < 1e-9, f"Growth is (812 - 700) / 4 = 28 pupils a year, so 2017 is 840. Got {f[2017]}"
assert abs(f[2026] - (812 + 10 * 28)) < 1e-9, "Ten years of 28 a year on top of 812"
hints: The loop is the chapter's loop with different start and end: for t in linrange(t_end, end_year):.
blocks.solution:
def forecast(series, end_year):
    t_0, t_end = get_first_label(series), get_last_label(series)
    growth = (get_last_value(series) - get_first_value(series)) / (t_end - t_0)
    results = TimeSeries()
    results[t_end] = get_last_value(series)
    for t in linrange(t_end, end_year):
        results[t + 1] = results[t] + growth
    return results

chapters.title: Modeling growth
chapters.tagline: System objects, proportional growth, and factoring out the update function
goals: Bundle parameters into a System object
Write a proportional growth model: growth = alpha × population
Factor out an update function so one run_simulation serves many models
Combine birth and death rates into a net growth rate

blocks.html: As models grow, functions need more parameters. We collect them in a System object, so a function takes one argument and reads what it needs.

blocks.code:
system = System(t_0=1950, t_end=2016, p_0=2.558, annual_growth=0.0723)
print(system)
print(system.t_end - system.t_0, "years")
blocks.title: A System

blocks.code:
system = System(t_0=2000, t_end=2010, p_0=6.0, alpha=0.01)
print(system.t_end - system.t_0)
print(round(system.p_0 * (1 + system.alpha), 3))

blocks.html: People have children, and more people have more children. So maybe growth is proportional to population: each year, population increases by alpha × population, where alpha is the net growth rate (births minus deaths, per person per year).

Every model in this part has the same loop; only the rule for "next year from this year" changes. We separate the rule into an update function and writes one run_simulation that takes the rule as an argument.

blocks.title: run_simulation with an update function
blocks.prompt: Write run_simulation(system, update_func): start a TimeSeries at system.t_0 with system.p_0, and for each year in linrange(system.t_0, system.t_end) set the next value to update_func(results[t], t, system). Return the TimeSeries.
blocks.tests:
sys1 = System(t_0=0, t_end=3, p_0=1.0)
r = run_simulation(sys1, lambda pop, t, system: pop * 2)
assert r.tolist() == [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0], f"Doubling for 3 steps: [1, 2, 4, 8], got {r.tolist()}"
assert list(r.index) == [0, 1, 2, 3], "Times 0 to t_end inclusive"
blocks.starter:
def run_simulation(system, update_func):
    pass

blocks.title: update_func for proportional growth
blocks.prompt: Fill in the update function for proportional growth.
blocks.tests:
s = System(alpha=0.1)
assert abs(update_func1(10.0, 0, s) - 11.0) < 1e-9, "10% of 10 is 1, so next year is 11"
assert update_func1(0.0, 0, s) == 0, "No people, no growth"

blocks.code:
def run_simulation(system, update_func):
    results = TimeSeries()
    results[system.t_0] = system.p_0
    for t in linrange(system.t_0, system.t_end):
        results[t + 1] = update_func(results[t], t, system)
    return results

def update_func1(pop, t, system):
    return pop + system.alpha * pop

system = System(t_0=1950, t_end=2016, p_0=census[1950], alpha=0.017)
results = run_simulation(system, update_func1)
plot(census, "o", label="US Census")
plot(results, color="gray", label="proportional growth, alpha = 0.017")
decorate(xlabel="Year", ylabel="World population (billion)")
print("model in 2016:", round(results[2016], 2), "  data:", census[2016])
blocks.title: Proportional growth vs data

blocks.html: Change alpha. Can you find a value that fits the whole curve? (You can't: proportional growth is exponential, and it bends the wrong way after about 1990.)
Writing alpha as one number hides two processes. So we split it into a birth rate and a death rate.

blocks.name: ms-pop-prop
blocks.title: Births minus deaths
blocks.goal: Set the birth and death rates to get an RMS error under 220 million, then compare with constant growth.
blocks.intro: Population grows by (births − deaths) × population each year.

blocks.title: Births and deaths
blocks.prompt: Write update_func2(pop, t, system) using system.birth_rate and system.death_rate (both per person per year).
blocks.tests:
s = System(birth_rate=0.03, death_rate=0.01)
assert abs(update_func2(100.0, 0, s) - 102.0) < 1e-9, "3 born, 1 dies per 100: 102"
assert abs(update_func2(50.0, 0, System(birth_rate=0.01, death_rate=0.01)) - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Equal rates: no change"
blocks.starter:
def update_func2(pop, t, system):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def update_func2(pop, t, system):
    births = system.birth_rate * pop
    deaths = system.death_rate * pop
    return pop + births - deaths

blocks.html: Proportional growth with births and deaths isn't only for people. sections.title: Growth slows as the world fills

blocks.html:
Proportional growth keeps accelerating, but the data show growth slowing. One explanation: as population rises, resources get scarcer, so the growth rate falls. The simplest way to model that is to make the net growth depend on p²:

net growth = alpha·p + beta·p²

with alpha > 0 (people have children) and beta < 0 (crowding slows growth). Typical values: alpha = 0.025, beta = −0.0018.

blocks.q: What's the equilibrium of the quadratic model, why does the model have one, and is it stable?
blocks.a:
• Net growth alpha·p + beta·p² is zero at p = −alpha/beta (≈ 13.9 billion with these values).
  • Because beta < 0, crowding grows faster than births as p rises, so growth hits zero.
  • It's stable: above it net growth is negative, below it positive, so the population moves toward it.

sections.title: Real-world project: a safe fishing quota for a lake

blocks.html: The quadratic model is the standard starting point for managing fish, deer and forests. A lake has a carrying capacity, and the stock grows fastest when it is about half full (that's where alpha·p + beta·p² is biggest). Take out a fixed catch every year and the equilibrium moves. Take out too much and there's no equilibrium left at all: the stock collapses. The model tells you where that cliff edge is.

blocks.why: Fisheries really do set quotas from this model (it's called the maximum sustainable yield). The software pattern is broader: subtract a constant drain from a self-replenishing resource and look for the tipping point. It's the same shape as a cache under load, a battery being topped up by solar, or a support team with a backlog that grows faster than they can clear it.

sections.title: Where did alpha and beta come from?

blocks.html:
The quadratic model says the growth rate per person is a straight line in p:

net growth / p = alpha + beta·p

So if we compute the growth rate from the data and plot it against population, the intercept is alpha and the slope is beta. That's an estimate from data, not a guess.

blocks.solution:
def growth_rates(series):
    t = np.array(series.index, dtype=float)
    p = np.array(series.values, dtype=float)
    rates = np.diff(p) / np.diff(t) / p[:-1]
    return p[:-1], rates

sections.title: Real-world project: when will the storage cluster be full?

blocks.html: Fitting alpha and beta from data is how you turn "it's growing fast" into a date. A company's file storage grows like a population: more users store more files, but growth slows as the market fills up. def fit_alpha_beta(series):
    t = np.array(series.index, dtype=float)
    p = np.array(series.values, dtype=float)
    rates = np.diff(p) / np.diff(t) / p[:-1]
    beta, alpha = np.polyfit(p[:-1], rates, 1)

blocks.html:
The proportional growth model as a recurrence relation (discrete steps):

x(n+1) = x(n) + α·x(n)

As a differential equation (continuous time), the change per unit time is proportional to x:

dx/dt = α·x

Its solution is exponential growth: x(t) = x₀·e^(αt). For the discrete version, x(n) = x₀·(1+α)ⁿ.

Simulation handles models that have no closed form. Good modelers use both, and check one against the other.

blocks.q: When would you use analysis rather than simulation, and vice versa?
blocks.a:
• Analysis (closed-form solutions) gives insight into how results depend on parameters, and is fast for any time or input, but only exists for some models.
  • Simulation works for almost any model (nonlinear, random, complicated) but gives one numerical answer per run and less insight.
  • Check one against the other when both are possible.

blocks.setup:
def simulate_lanes(lam, mu, c, minutes=4000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x, total = 0, 0
    for t in range(minutes):
        busy = min(x, c)
        x -= rng.binomial(busy, mu)
        x += rng.poisson(lam)
        total += x
    L = total / minutes
    return L / lam

blocks.html:
Every fall at Olin College, a few days after the first-years arrive, an illness spreads through the class. We model it with the classic SIR model: everyone is in one of three compartments.

  • Susceptible: can catch it.
  • Infectious: has it and can spread it.
  • Recovered: had it, now immune.

Two parameters drive the flow S → I → R:

  • β (beta), the contact rate: each infected person makes β infecting contacts per day, but only contacts with susceptible people count, so new infections per day = β·i·s.
  • γ (gamma), the recovery rate: a fraction γ of infected people recover each day, so recoveries = γ·i. If illness lasts about 4 days, γ = 1/4.

We use fractions of the population (s + i + r = 1). The class has 90 students, one of them sick on day 0.

blocks.q: Why is the number of new infections proportional to s·i and not just to i?

opts.t: An infection needs a contact between an infectious person and a susceptible one; as susceptibles run out, contacts stop producing infections
Because recovered people get sick again

blocks.why: Each infectious person's contacts are spread over the whole population, and only the fraction s of them can be infected. That s·i product is what eventually stops the epidemic.

blocks.solution:
def update_func(state, t, system):
    s, i, r = state
    infected = system.beta * i * s
    recovered = system.gamma * i
    s -= infected
    i += infected - recovered
    r += recovered
    return State(S=s, I=i, R=r)

blocks.starter:
def update_func(state, t, system):
    s, i, r = state
    infected = system.beta * i
    recovered = system.gamma * i
    s -= infected
    i += infected - recovered
    r += recovered
    return State(S=s, I=i, R=r)
blocks.solution:
def update_func(state, t, system):
    s, i, r = state
    infected = system.beta * i * s
    recovered = system.gamma * i
    s -= infected
    i += infected - recovered
    r += recovered
    return State(S=s, I=i, R=r)

blocks.q: Describe the SIR model: compartments, parameters, and the flow equations for one day.
blocks.a:
• Compartments S, I, R as fractions of the population.
  • β: contact rate (infecting contacts per infected person per day); γ: recovery rate (1 / days sick).
  • Each day: infected = β·i·s moves from S to I; recovered = γ·i moves from I to R.
  • The total s + i + r stays 1.

Dividing the S and R equations and integrating gives a relation between c and the final fraction of susceptibles, s∞, for an outbreak that starts with almost everyone susceptible:

We can't easily solve for s∞, but going the other way is easy, and that's enough to plot it.

sections.title: Real-world project: an outbreak planner for a campus clinic

blocks.html: The final-size equation is more than a neat formula. If you can guess c for a disease (from last year's outbreak, say), it tells you how many people will get sick in total before anyone runs a single simulation. That's exactly the number a clinic needs to plan beds, staff and how many people to vaccinate.

The relation c = ln(s∞)/(s∞ − 1) goes from s∞ to c; your tool needs the other direction, so you'll solve it with a root finder.
blocks.why: Public-health teams do this every season: the "attack rate" (fraction who get sick) from the final-size relation is the first estimate in pandemic plans, school-closure decisions and vaccine orders. In software terms you're turning an equation you can't rearrange into a function you can call, which is the same trick behind loan calculators (solve for the interest rate) and game physics (solve for the launch speed).

chapters.tagline: The coffee cooling problem and Newton's law of cooling
goals: Distinguish temperature from heat, and name the three ways heat moves

blocks.html: You order coffee and a little cup of cold milk. You want to drink it in a few minutes, as hot as possible. Should you add the milk now or just before drinking? This chapter builds the cooling model; chapter 16 answers the question.

Heat is energy; temperature measures how hot something is. Adding heat Q to a mass m raises its temperature by ΔT = Q / (m·c), where c is the specific heat capacity (for water, about 4.2 J/g/°C). Heat moves by conduction (through the cup), convection (air carrying it away) and radiation.

blocks.html:
All three mechanisms are complicated, so we use a simple empirical law: the rate of cooling is proportional to the difference between the object's temperature and its environment:

dT/dt = −r·(T − T_env)

r depends on the cup, the liquid and the air; we'll estimate it from a measurement.

blocks.q: State Newton's law of cooling and explain how it becomes an update function.
blocks.a:
• dT/dt = −r(T − T_env): cooling rate proportional to the temperature difference with the surroundings.

  • r is fitted to a measurement (e.g. 70 °C after 30 min); the time step must multiply the rate.

blocks.html: Pharmacokinetics studies how substances move through the body. Part II's biggest case study is the frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test (FSIGT): a patient fasts, gets an injection of glucose, and doctors measure blood glucose and insulin every few minutes. How fast glucose returns to normal tells you how well insulin works, which matters for diagnosing diabetes.

blocks.title: The measurements

blocks.html:
Bergman's glucose minimal model has two state variables: glucose concentration G and X, the effect of insulin in the tissues ("remote insulin"). Insulin concentration I(t) comes from the measurements.

  • dG/dt = −k₁·(G − G_b) − X·G
  • dX/dt = k₃·(I(t) − I_b) − k₂·X

G_b and I_b are the basal (fasting) levels. k₁ is how fast glucose falls back on its own; X·G is the extra uptake caused by insulin; k₂ and k₃ control how remote insulin rises and decays.

blocks.q: If a patient's tissues respond weakly to insulin (insulin resistance), which parameter in the model would be small?

blocks.prompt: Write update_func(state, t, system). Unpack G, X = state, compute the two derivatives from the equations above (use system.I(t)), and take one Euler step of size system.dt. Return State(G=..., X=...).

blocks.solution:
def update_func(state, t, system):
    G, X = state
    k1, k2, k3 = system.k1, system.k2, system.k3
    I, Ib, Gb = system.I, system.Ib, system.Gb
    dGdt = -k1 * (G - Gb) - X * G
    dXdt = k3 * (I(t) - Ib) - k2 * X
    G += dGdt * system.dt
    X += dXdt * system.dt
    return State(G=G, X=X)

def update_func(state, t, system):
    G, X = state
    dGdt = -system.k1 * (G - system.Gb) - X * G
    dXdt = system.k3 * (system.I(t) - system.Ib) - system.k2 * X

def run_simulation(system, update_func):

    return frame

blocks.html: You just turned sparse lab samples into a smooth function with interpolate. blocks.html: Our update functions took an Euler step themselves, with a fixed dt. The next step hands that job to a proper ODE solver. You write only a slope function: given the state and time, return the derivatives. run_ode_solver(system, slope_func) chooses its own step sizes (smaller where things change fast) and returns a TimeFrame plus details.

def slope_func(state, t, system):
    G, X = state

    dGdt = -k1 * (G - Gb) - X * G

    return dGdt, dXdt

blocks.q: Why use an ODE solver instead of the Euler loop from chapter 17?

opts.t: Euler can't handle two state variables
The solver adapts its step size and uses better methods, so it's more accurate for the same work, and you only write the derivatives

blocks.why: Euler with a fixed dt has an error that shrinks only in proportion to dt. Adaptive solvers (scipy's RK45 here) take small steps where things change fast and big ones where they don't, and they control the error for you.

blocks.html: Where did k₁, k₂, k₃ and G₀ come from? We fit them: choose the values that make the model's G closest to the data. The standard measure is the sum of squared errors (model − data). fit_leastsq(error_func, params, data) searches for the parameters that minimise it.

blocks.q: What's the difference between an update function and a slope function, and how do you fit a model's parameters?
blocks.a:
• An update function computes the next state itself (e.g. an Euler step with fixed dt). A slope function only returns derivatives; the ODE solver decides how to step.
  • Fitting: write an error function returning model − data for given parameters; a least-squares optimiser (fit_leastsq) adjusts the parameters to minimise the sum of squared errors.

The glucose model took insulin as measured input. A companion model explains insulin itself: the pancreas secretes insulin when glucose is above a threshold G_T, and the body clears it at rate k.

dI/dt = −k·I + γ·max(G(t) − G_T, 0)·t

blocks.html:
An electronic RC circuit (a resistor R and a capacitor C) smooths a signal: slow changes pass through, fast wiggles get damped. The output voltage follows

dV_out/dt = (V_in(t) − V_out) / (R·C)

That's Newton's law of cooling again, with V_in as a moving "room temperature". The cutoff frequency is f_c = 1 / (2π·R·C).

sections.title: Real-world project: a steady display for a kitchen scale

blocks.html: The RC filter is everywhere in software too, as a few lines of code. A digital scale's load sensor jitters by a few grams, so the raw number on the display flickers. Run the readings through a low-pass filter and the display goes steady, but if you smooth too much it takes ages to show a new weight. Picking R·C is picking that trade-off.

blocks.client: A company making a Bluetooth kitchen scale with a companion recipe app

blocks.why: This exact filter (often called an exponential moving average) smooths phone accelerometers, game-controller sticks, audio volume meters, stock-price indicators and the "estimated time remaining" in file downloads. Each one picks a time constant to trade smoothness against lag, which is the same number as R·C here.

chapters.title: Projectiles
chapters.tagline: Newton's second law as two first-order equations, and events that stop a simulation
goals: Turn a second-order equation (acceleration) into two first-order ones (position and velocity)
Simulate the falling penny with run_ode_solver
Use an event function to stop exactly when the penny hits the ground

blocks.html:
Part II's systems had first derivatives: temperature changes at some rate. Mechanics is different. Newton's second law, F = m·a, gives the acceleration, the second derivative of position. The trick: track two state variables, position y and velocity v:

  • dy/dt = v
  • dv/dt = a = F/m

Now it's two first-order equations, and run_ode_solver can handle it.

blocks.q: To simulate a falling object with run_ode_solver, what goes in the state?
blocks.why: The slope function must return the derivative of every state variable. Position's derivative is velocity (which must therefore be in the state) and velocity's derivative is acceleration (computed from forces).

blocks.q: How do we turn Newton's second law into something run_ode_solver can solve, and how does it stop at the ground?
blocks.a:
• Use position and velocity as state variables: dy/dt = v, dv/dt = F/m (here −g). Two first-order ODEs instead of one second-order one.

sections.title: Real-world project: a drop-tower ride designer

blocks.html: A penny falling from a building is a thought experiment; a drop tower at a theme park is the same physics on purpose. Riders fall freely, then magnetic brakes stop them. The designer's questions are the ones you can now answer with an event: at what height does the car reach its top speed, and is there enough tower left below it to brake?

chapters.title: Air resistance
chapters.tagline: Drag, terminal velocity, and the penny myth finally busted
goals: Use the drag equation and explain each of its terms
Work backward from a measured terminal velocity to a drag coefficient
Add drag to the falling-penny model and compare with chapter 20
chapters.prelude:
from modsim import *

def event_func(state, t, system):
    y, v = state
    return y

blocks.html:
Moving through air, an object pushes air aside and feels a force opposite to its motion:

F_drag = ½ · ρ · v² · C_d · A

  • ρ (rho): air density, about 1.2 kg/m³
  • v: speed (drag grows with its square)
  • C_d: the drag coefficient, set by shape (measured, not derived)
  • A: the cross-sectional area facing the air

As the penny speeds up, drag grows until it equals gravity's pull. Then acceleration is zero and the speed stays constant: terminal velocity.

blocks.q: If you double an object's speed, what happens to its drag force?

opts.t: Nothing; drag depends only on shape

blocks.why: Drag is proportional to v², so 2× the speed gives 4× the force. That's why terminal velocity arrives fairly quickly for light objects.

blocks.html: Measurements say a penny's terminal velocity is about 18 m/s. At terminal velocity drag equals weight: ½ρv²C_dA = m·g. Solve for C_d.

blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    y, v = state
    rho, C_d, g = system.rho, system.C_d, system.g
    area, mass = system.area, system.mass
    f_drag = rho * v**2 * C_d * area / 2
    a_drag = f_drag / mass
    dydt = v
    dvdt = -g + a_drag
    return dydt, dvdt

blocks.q: What is terminal velocity, and how did we use it to find the penny's drag coefficient?
blocks.a:
• The speed at which drag equals weight, so acceleration is zero and speed stops changing.
  • Setting ½ρv²C_dA = mg at the measured terminal velocity (18 m/s) gives C_d = 2mg/(ρAv²) ≈ 0.44 for a penny.

sections.title: Real-world project: a parachute sizer for a weather-balloon payload

blocks.html: You worked backward from a terminal velocity to a drag coefficient. Engineers do the same thing in the other direction all the time: pick the landing speed you want, then solve for the parachute. Too small and the payload smashes; too big and it drifts kilometres in the wind and costs more. Terminal velocity is the bridge between the two.

blocks.solution:
def drag_force(V, system):
    rho, C_d, area = system.rho, system.C_d, system.area
    mag = rho * V.mag**2 * C_d * area / 2
    direction = -V.hat()
    return direction * mag

blocks.q: How do you write drag for 2-D motion with Vectors?

• Magnitude ½ρ|V|²C_dA, same as 1-D.

blocks.q: Describe the two-level search the Manny Ramirez problem uses.
blocks.a:
• Inner: for a given speed, maximize searches over launch angle (each evaluation runs a full simulation) to find the best angle.
  • Outer: root_bisect searches over speed for the value where the ball's height at the wall, at its best angle, equals the wall's height.
  • Each level wraps a simulation in a function of one parameter, so standard optimizers and root finders can drive it.

blocks.html: The Manny Ramirez problem is really a pattern: wrap a simulation in a function, let an optimizer pick the best angle, then let a root finder pick the smallest speed that reaches a target. A lawn sprinkler is the same pattern with tiny, drag-dominated water drops instead of a baseball, so the answers come out very differently.

sections.title: Rotation, the same way as motion

blocks.html: A spinning object has an angle θ (radians) and an angular velocity ω = dθ/dt (radians per second). A point at radius r on the rim moves at linear speed v = r·ω. One full turn is 2π radians.

blocks.code:
r, omega = 0.05, 10           # metres, radians per second
print(r * omega)               # rim speed in m/s
print(round(2 * pi / omega, 3)) # seconds per turn

blocks.html:
The example: a roll of toilet paper with core radius R_min = 2 cm, full radius R_max = 5.5 cm, and paper length L = 47 m. If you pull it so the roll turns at a constant ω = 10 rad/s, how long until it's empty?

As paper comes off, the radius shrinks, so each turn delivers less paper. Each turn removes a layer of thickness k·2π, where k comes from the geometry: the area of the paper's cross-section (π(R_max² − R_min²)) equals its length times its thickness, giving

k = (R_max² − R_min²) / (2L)

blocks.q: How does the toilet paper model connect rotation to linear motion?
blocks.a:
• The rim moves at v = r·ω, so paper comes off at dy/dt = r·ω.
  • Each radian unrolled removes thickness k, so dr/dt = −k·ω with k = (R_max² − R_min²)/(2L).
  • With constant ω, θ grows steadily while the paper comes out more slowly as r shrinks; an event stops at y = L.

sections.title: Real-world project: a constant-speed reel controller

blocks.html: The toilet-paper roll turned at a constant ω, so the paper came off slower and slower as the radius shrank. Real machines that unwind paper, film, labels or cable usually need the opposite: a constant line speed, so the motor has to spin faster as the roll gets smaller. That's v = r·ω, solved for ω, running in a loop.

"Estimate what's left from one easy measurement" is the same idea as a fuel gauge, or a phone estimating battery charge from voltage.

blocks.solution:
def time_to_empty(R_min, R_max, L, v_line):
    k = (R_max**2 - R_min**2) / (2 * L)

    def slope_func(state, t, system):
        y, r = state
        omega = system.v_line / r
        return system.v_line, -system.k * omega

    def event_func(state, t, system):
        y, r = state
        return r - R_min

    system = System(init=State(y=0.0, r=R_max), k=k, v_line=v_line, t_end=10 * L / v_line)
    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    return get_last_label(results), v_line / R_min

chapters.title: Torque
chapters.tagline: Newton's law for rotation, moment of inertia, and a teapot on a spinning turntable
goals: Use τ = I·α, the rotational version of F = m·a
Compute the moment of inertia of a disk and of a point mass
Simulate a turntable pushed and then slowed by friction, and estimate the friction from data

blocks.html:
A torque τ (force × lever arm, N·m) causes angular acceleration α:

τ = I·α

I is the moment of inertia, rotation's version of mass. It depends on how far the mass sits from the axis:

  • a solid disk of mass m, radius r: I = ½·m·r²
  • a small mass m at distance r: I = m·r²

blocks.q: Two disks have the same mass, but one has twice the radius. Compared with the smaller one, how much torque does it need for the same angular acceleration?
blocks.why: I = ½mr², so doubling r quadruples I, and τ = Iα needs four times the torque. Mass far from the axis is hard to spin.

blocks.html: The setup: a turntable (a disk, 7 kg, radius 0.5 m) with a teapot (0.3 kg) near the edge at 0.4 m. You push the edge with a force of 2 N for 0.5 s, then let go. Friction exerts a constant opposing torque until it stops.

Friction torque system.tau_friction always opposes motion while omega > 0 (use 0 when it isn't moving). Return (omega, alpha) with alpha = net_torque / system.I.

blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    theta, omega = state
    tau = system.force * system.radius if t < system.t_push else 0
    if omega > 0:
        tau -= system.tau_friction
    alpha = tau / system.I
    return omega, alpha

sections.title: Real-world project: motor sizing for a product-photo turntable

blocks.html: The teapot model takes a torque and tells you how the turntable moves. A product designer asks the reverse: which motor is strong enough? Real motors don't give a constant torque; a small DC motor pushes hardest when it's stopped and its torque falls to zero at its top speed. With that one change, a hand formula no longer works, and the simulation earns its keep.

blocks.client: An online shop building motorised turntables for 360° product photos

The camera wants one turn every 10 seconds (0.63 rad/s), reached within 2 seconds of pressing start. Candidate motors have different stall torques and free speeds. Build the tool: compute I, simulate the spin-up with the motor's torque curve and friction, and report the time to reach speed, or that the motor never gets there.
blocks.why: Sizing a motor against a load's inertia is daily work for robotics, e-bike, drone, conveyor and hard-drive engineers, and spec sheets give exactly these two numbers (stall torque and no-load speed). The software lesson: when an input depends on the state (torque depends on ω), you can't use the simple formula, but the slope function doesn't care.

The final case study: a jumper leaps from a crane 80 m up, attached to a bungee cord 25 m long. The stunt is to dip into a cup of tea at the very bottom (a "bungee dunk"). What spring constant should the cord have so the jumper's lowest point is exactly at the ground?

def slope_func(state, t, system):
    y, v = state
    a_drag = -system.C_d_term * v * abs(v)
    a_spring = spring_force(y, system) / system.mass
    a = -system.g + a_drag + a_spring
    return v, a

sections.title: Real-world project: a cord-length safety calculator for an adventure park

blocks.html: The bungee dunk aimed for a lowest point of exactly zero. A real jump operator wants the opposite of a dunk: a guaranteed gap above the ground, for every jumper, whatever they weigh. Heavier jumpers stretch the cord further, so parks keep a table of cord lengths by weight class. You can compute that table with the model you just built.

blocks.title: Bungee cord-length safety table
blocks.client: An adventure park running a bungee jump from an 80 m bridge
blocks.brief: The park uses one cord stiffness (k = 60 N/m) but can fit different cord lengths. Every jumper is weighed. For each weight class the operator needs the longest cord (the most thrilling jump) that still keeps the jumper's lowest point at least 5 m above the ground. Also report the peak pull of the cord in g's, which must stay comfortable.
blocks.why: Safety-critical calculators like this sit behind ride operations, crane load charts, climbing-rope ratings and elevator design: a physics model wrapped in a search, with a safety margin, turned into a lookup table that staff can use without running code. The engineering habit is the same everywhere: compute the limit, then build in a margin, and test the extremes (the heaviest jumper) first.
